resume-apply:0.prompt: Which resume bullet is strongest for a senior backend role?
options: Responsible for working on the payments service and fixing bugs
Worked with Node.js, Redis, Kafka, PostgreSQL and Docker across many payment and checkout features
Cut payment API p99 latency from 1.2s to 300ms with Redis caching and batched writes, lifting conversion 3%
Helped the team significantly improve the performance and reliability of various backend services in production
resume-apply:0.explanation: It names an action, the technical how, and measurable before/after impact tied to business value. A tool list shows exposure, not outcomes, and 'significantly' without numbers is unverifiable.

resume-apply:0.prompt: What is the widely used structure for an impact bullet (often phrased as the 'XYZ' formula)?
options: Accomplished X, as measured by Y, by doing Z
Job title, company, dates
Technology used, its version, and your years of experience with it
Problem, apology, lesson learned
resume-apply:0.explanation: 'Accomplished X as measured by Y by doing Z' forces outcome, metric and method into one line. Title/company/dates is header information, not a bullet structure.

resume-apply:0.prompt: You led a migration but have no exact latency numbers. What's the best way to still quantify impact honestly?
options: Invent plausible round numbers, since recruiters rarely check and metrics make bullets stand out
Leave every metric out and describe your responsibilities in detail, so nothing can be questioned later
Write 'massively improved everything'
Use numbers you can defend: scale (requests/day, records migrated), scope, or explainable estimates
resume-apply:0.explanation: Scale and scope numbers, or clearly explainable estimates, quantify impact without fabrication. Interviewers probe numbers, so invented metrics collapse under one follow-up question.

resume-apply:0.prompt: Which verb choice best signals ownership in a bullet?
options: 'Was involved in' the design of the notification service handling 2M pushes/day
'Designed and shipped' the notification service handling 2M pushes/day
'Participated in' the notification service project
'Exposed to' notification service development
resume-apply:0.explanation: Strong action verbs ('designed', 'led', 'reduced') state what you did. 'Involved in' or 'participated in' hide your contribution and make reviewers assume a minor role.

resume-apply:0.prompt: A bullet says 'Reduced AWS costs by 40%'. What is the interviewer most likely to probe?
options: Your baseline and absolute figures, what you specifically changed, and how you measured the result
Your favourite AWS region
Whether you hold an AWS certification that qualifies you to make cost decisions on production cloud accounts
How many hours you worked that week
resume-apply:0.explanation: Metrics invite verification: from what to what, which levers (rightsizing, reserved capacity, caching), your role versus the team's, and how it was measured. Be ready to defend every number.

resume-apply:0.prompt: Which bullet best balances technical depth with business impact?
options: Built an idempotent webhook processor (outbox pattern), ending ~150 duplicate charges/month and their tickets
Implemented the outbox pattern
Improved customer happiness and reduced support load through better engineering practices across the payments team
Used design patterns and SOLID principles to write clean, maintainable code in the webhooks module
resume-apply:0.explanation: It names the technique (signals seniority to engineers) and the business result (signals value to managers). The bare 'outbox pattern' line lacks impact; the others lack specifics.

resume-apply:0.prompt: Your 'Experience' section has 9 bullets for your current role, several describing routine tasks. What's the best edit for a senior role?
options: Keep all 9 to show you're busy
Add more bullets so every technology you used is covered, since recruiters search for keywords
Cut to the 4-6 highest-impact, most role-relevant bullets, ordered by impact
Move everything into one long paragraph
resume-apply:0.explanation: Recruiters skim quickly; fewer, stronger bullets ranked by impact and relevance make your best work visible. Routine tasks dilute signal, and a dense paragraph is harder to scan.

resume-apply:0.prompt: Which kinds of metrics make good evidence in backend resume bullets? Select all that apply.
options: Latency or throughput changes (p95, RPS)
Reliability changes (error rate, incidents, uptime)
Cost savings or engineering hours saved
Number of meetings attended
resume-apply:0.explanation: Performance, reliability and cost/time metrics map directly to backend value. Meetings attended measure activity, not impact.

resume-apply:0.prompt: Which are common mistakes in resume bullets? Select all that apply.
options: Listing duties ('responsible for...') instead of results
Claiming team results as solely your own when you can't explain them
Using metrics you can explain in detail
Vague adjectives like 'significantly' or 'various' without specifics
resume-apply:0.explanation: Duties, overclaiming and vagueness all weaken bullets. Metrics you can explain in depth are exactly what you want.

resume-apply:0.prompt: Adding relevant keywords from the job description (where they truthfully describe your work) can help a resume pass applicant tracking system (ATS) screening and recruiter skims.
options: True
False
resume-apply:0.explanation: True. Recruiters and ATS filters search for the role's terms (e.g. 'Node.js', 'PostgreSQL', 'microservices'). Use them where accurate, inside impact bullets rather than keyword-stuffed lists.

resume-apply:0.prompt: For a senior engineer, a longer list of technologies in the skills section is more persuasive than a few quantified achievements.
options: True
False
resume-apply:0.explanation: False. Senior hiring is about judgement and impact. Demonstrated results with depth outweigh breadth of exposure; huge tool lists also invite questions you may not be able to answer deeply.

resume-apply:1.prompt: Which resume bullet best presents a personal Next.js + MongoDB interview-prep app with LLM-generated quizzes?
options: Made a study app for myself using lots of modern tech
Built a modern full-stack application with Next.js, MongoDB, AI, React, TypeScript, Tailwind, Vercel and more
Built a Next.js + MongoDB prep platform with LLM quizzes validated by zod, falling back to a curated bank
Created an app that uses ChatGPT to make quizzes, very useful
resume-apply:1.explanation: It shows the stack plus engineering decisions (validation of untrusted output, graceful degradation). 'Next.js app with MongoDB and AI' is accurate but says nothing about design judgement.

resume-apply:1.prompt: An interviewer asks: 'Why validate LLM output with a schema before saving it?' What's the strongest answer?
options: LLM output is untrusted and can be malformed or wrong; validation keeps bad data out of the DB and UI
Because the linter requires it
To make the LLM respond faster
Because MongoDB rejects JSON that hasn't been validated against a schema before it is inserted into a collection
resume-apply:1.explanation: Treating model output like any untrusted input (validate, then cache only valid results) shows mature engineering. MongoDB will store arbitrary documents happily, which is exactly why app-level validation matters.

resume-apply:1.prompt: The project uses a scheduled cron job to prepare each day's plan, and also generates the day on dashboard load if cron didn't run. How should you describe this design on the resume or in an interview?
options: 'Used cron jobs'
An idempotent daily job with a lazy on-demand fallback, so the app stays correct if a scheduled run is missed
As a real-time event streaming pipeline that recomputes the plan whenever any underlying data changes
As a microservices architecture
resume-apply:1.explanation: Describing the reliability property (idempotent generation, works without cron) highlights backend thinking. 'Used cron jobs' undersells it, and calling it streaming or microservices misrepresents it.

resume-apply:1.prompt: An interviewer asks why the app computes 'today' in a configured timezone instead of using server-local time. What's the best explanation?
options: Server-local time is slower to compute because every request must first load and parse the host's timezone database
Timezones are required by Next.js
Serverless functions usually run in UTC, so day boundaries would be off; an app timezone keeps streaks consistent
It makes the database smaller
resume-apply:1.explanation: Day-boundary bugs are a classic issue: a serverless function in UTC would roll over at 5:30am IST. Explaining this shows awareness of real production pitfalls. It isn't about speed or framework requirements.

resume-apply:1.prompt: Where should this side project go on a resume for someone with 4+ years of backend experience?
options: At the top, above all work experience, because it shows initiative and is the most recent thing you've personally built
Only in the cover letter
Hidden in the skills section as a keyword
In a concise 'Projects' section after experience, with 1-3 bullets on its hardest engineering decisions
resume-apply:1.explanation: For experienced engineers, professional work leads; a project section adds signal, especially for skills (LLM integration) not shown at work. Putting it above experience suggests the job experience is weak.

resume-apply:1.prompt: The app runs entirely on free tiers (serverless hosting, a free MongoDB cluster, free LLM tiers). Which framing turns that constraint into a strength?
options: Designed within free-tier limits: connection reuse, provider fallbacks, caching only validated AI output
It's free so it isn't a serious project
Leave hosting out entirely, since mentioning free tiers suggests the project isn't production-grade or serious
Claim it's built to handle millions of users
resume-apply:1.explanation: Constraints force engineering choices (connection management, caching, fallbacks) that interviewers value. Inflating scale to 'millions of users' for a single-user app is a credibility risk.

resume-apply:1.prompt: An interviewer asks, 'How would this design change if it had 100k users?' What does a strong answer focus on?
options: 'It would work the same; Next.js scales automatically'
Switching to a different programming language
Concrete limits: multi-user auth, per-user indexes, queued generation instead of cron, LLM quotas and caching
Rewrite everything as microservices immediately, one per feature, each with its own database and deployment
resume-apply:1.explanation: This probes whether you understand the limits of your own design. Naming specific bottlenecks (auth, data model, job processing, LLM quotas) shows judgement; claiming automatic scaling or reflexive rewrites doesn't.

resume-apply:1.prompt: Which details from this project are worth highlighting for a senior Node.js backend role? Select all that apply.
options: Treating LLM output as untrusted: schema validation and caching only validated results
Graceful degradation when no LLM key or cron is available
Business logic in pure, unit-tested domain functions separate from I/O services
The colour palette used in the UI
resume-apply:1.explanation: Validation, resilience and testable architecture are backend signals. UI colours aren't relevant to a backend role, though they could matter for a frontend one.

resume-apply:1.prompt: What should you prepare before listing this project on your resume? Select all that apply.
options: A short architecture walkthrough you can sketch in 2-3 minutes
The trade-offs you made and what you'd change
A clean public repo or demo, with secrets removed
A memorised list of every npm dependency version
resume-apply:1.explanation: Anything on a resume is fair game: be ready to explain architecture and trade-offs and to show code safely. Dependency versions are trivia nobody will ask about.

resume-apply:1.prompt: Describing a single-user personal tool as a 'scalable platform used by thousands' is acceptable resume polish.
options: True
False
resume-apply:1.explanation: False. That's misrepresentation, and a single follow-up ('how many users?') exposes it, damaging trust in the rest of your resume. Accurate framing of real engineering decisions is stronger.

resume-apply:1.prompt: A side project can be a strong signal for skills your day job doesn't show, such as LLM integration, provided you can discuss its design decisions in depth.
options: True
False
resume-apply:1.explanation: True. Projects fill gaps in your professional story, but only if you can go deep: why each choice, what failed, what you'd improve. Shallow tutorial-style projects add little.

resume-apply:2.prompt: Which LinkedIn headline is most effective for someone targeting senior backend roles?
options: Looking for opportunities
Software Engineer at Acme
Passionate coder | Tech enthusiast | Lifelong learner | Problem solver | Team player | Innovator
Senior Backend Engineer | Node.js, TypeScript, PostgreSQL | Distributed systems & payments
resume-apply:2.explanation: Recruiters search by role and keywords; a headline with target title, core stack and domain gets found and is instantly clear. Generic phrases contain no searchable signal.

resume-apply:2.prompt: What is the best way to ask a former colleague at a target company for a referral?
options: A short, specific note: role link/id, why you fit in 2-3 lines, and your resume, so it's easy to act on
Send just 'Hi' and wait for a reply
Ask them to find any job for you
Message ten people at the company with the same copy-paste text at once, to maximise the chance of a reply
resume-apply:2.explanation: Specific, low-effort asks get acted on: the referrer needs the job id, a fit summary, and your resume. Vague 'any job' asks push the work onto them and usually stall.

resume-apply:2.prompt: Why build an explicit target list of ~30 companies instead of applying to every opening you see?
options: Recruiters automatically reject candidates whose applications show up at more than 30 companies in a month
It lets you prioritise by fit, track referrals and follow-ups, and tailor applications to each company
Job portals only allow 30 applications
It guarantees an offer
resume-apply:2.explanation: A curated list turns a scattershot search into a pipeline you can manage: tiers, contacts, status, dates. No such hard limits exist, and nothing guarantees offers.

resume-apply:2.prompt: On job portals like Naukri where recruiters search profiles, what typically keeps your profile visible?
options: Leaving it untouched after creation
Using a creative job title nobody searches for
A complete, keyword-rich profile with current skills, accurate experience and notice period, updated regularly
Uploading scanned photos of your certificates instead of a resume, since recruiters trust verified documents more
resume-apply:2.explanation: Recruiter search relies on keywords, completeness and recency. Stale or creatively titled profiles don't match searches. Specific ranking rules vary, but completeness and freshness consistently help.

resume-apply:2.prompt: Your LinkedIn 'About' section should mainly do what?
options: Repeat your full resume word for word so recruiters see the same details without having to open the attached PDF
List hobbies and favourite movies
Contain only a list of 40 skills
Summarise what you build, your strengths and impact, and the roles you're looking for, in a few lines
resume-apply:2.explanation: A concise narrative with impact and a clear target helps recruiters decide quickly to reach out. Copying the resume adds nothing, and skill lists belong in the Skills section.

resume-apply:2.prompt: You don't know anyone at 12 of your 30 target companies. What's the best next step?
options: Drop those companies from the list, since cold applications without a referral almost never get a response
Find second-degree connections or alumni there and send brief, specific messages; apply directly otherwise
Only apply through portals and never network
Ask strangers for referrals without reading the job post
resume-apply:2.explanation: Warm intros via mutual connections or alumni convert far better than cold asks, and direct applications remain a valid fallback. Dropping companies or blasting generic asks wastes opportunities.

resume-apply:2.prompt: Your resume says 'Senior Engineer, 2022-present' but LinkedIn still shows your old title and an extra job. Why does this matter?
options: It doesn't; recruiters never check LinkedIn
Inconsistencies between profiles and resume raise credibility questions during screening and background checks
LinkedIn automatically syncs your profile with uploaded resumes, so any mismatch gets corrected on its own within days
It only matters for frontend roles
resume-apply:2.explanation: Recruiters cross-check profiles; mismatched titles or dates look careless or deceptive and can surface in background verification. Keep every profile consistent with the resume.

resume-apply:2.prompt: What should a referral tracking sheet for your 30 companies include? Select all that apply.
options: Company, role and job link/id
Contact person and date you asked for a referral
Status and next follow-up date
Your guess of each interviewer's salary
resume-apply:2.explanation: Tracking role, contact, ask date, status and follow-ups stops leads from going cold. Guessing interviewers' salaries isn't useful.

resume-apply:2.prompt: Which LinkedIn practices help recruiters find and trust your profile? Select all that apply.
options: Experience entries with impact bullets matching your resume
A skills section featuring your core stack
Turning on recruiter-visible 'open to work' preferences with target roles and locations
Leaving the profile private and without a photo or headline
resume-apply:2.explanation: Consistent experience, relevant skills and open-to-work signals improve discoverability. A bare or hidden profile gives recruiters nothing to search or evaluate.

resume-apply:2.prompt: Referrals typically increase the chance that your application is seen by a human compared with a cold application through a careers page.
options: True
False
resume-apply:2.explanation: True. Referred candidates are commonly prioritised in screening because someone inside vouches for them. It doesn't skip the interview bar, but it gets your resume read.

resume-apply:2.prompt: Once someone agrees to refer you, it's best not to follow up even if you hear nothing for several weeks.
options: True
False
resume-apply:2.explanation: False. A polite follow-up after a week or two (thanking them and asking if the referral went through) is normal and often needed; referrals get lost in busy schedules.

resume-apply:3.prompt: You're starting to apply to 30 companies. What's the smartest sequencing strategy?
options: Apply to your dream companies first while you're most excited and motivated, then work your way down the list
Apply to everything on the same day
Warm up with a few lower-priority companies, then target top choices, timing offers to land close together
Apply only after you've finished all preparation, no matter how long it takes
resume-apply:3.explanation: Early interviews are practice; batching later ones lets offers overlap, improving negotiating leverage. Dream companies first risks spending your best shots before you've warmed up.

resume-apply:3.prompt: You've applied to 25 roles over 3 weeks and received zero callbacks. What should you examine first?
options: Your resume and targeting: impact-focused bullets, and roles whose level and stack actually match yours
Your LinkedIn profile picture
Whether interviewers like you
Your system design skills, since senior roles screen out candidates who can't design at scale on the first call
resume-apply:3.explanation: No callbacks means the funnel fails at screening, before any interview, so the resume, keywords, and role fit are the levers. Interview skills only matter once you get calls.

resume-apply:3.prompt: How much should you tailor your resume per application?
options: Write a completely new resume for every application
Never change anything
Change your job titles to match the posting's wording, so the ATS sees an exact title match for the role
Keep a strong base resume and tweak a few bullets and the summary to match each role's key requirements
resume-apply:3.explanation: Light tailoring (emphasis, keywords, ordering) gives most of the benefit at low cost. Changing actual job titles is misrepresentation, and full rewrites aren't sustainable at volume.

resume-apply:3.prompt: A recruiter asks for your expected salary on the first call, before you know the role's scope. What's a reasonable response?
options: Give a number well below your current salary to seem flexible, then negotiate upward once they make an offer
Ask to understand the role and level first and for their budgeted range; if pressed, give a researched range
Refuse to continue the conversation
State a random high number
resume-apply:3.explanation: Deferring until scope is clear, or anchoring with a researched range, protects your leverage. Lowballing can anchor the entire negotiation, and refusing outright can end the process.

resume-apply:3.prompt: You have a 90-day notice period. How does this affect your application strategy?
options: Hide it until the offer stage, since companies that like you enough will usually wait out the full period
Ignore it; companies never care
Disclose it upfront, ask about buyout or early release, and favour companies that accept longer notice
Apply only to companies that require immediate joiners
resume-apply:3.explanation: Notice period is a key screening factor for many employers; being upfront avoids wasted rounds and late surprises. Hiding it often causes offers to be withdrawn.

resume-apply:3.prompt: What is the main purpose of tracking each application's stage (applied, screen, technical, onsite, offer) in a spreadsheet?
options: To see where your funnel leaks (e.g. many screens but few onsite passes) and fix the right skill
To share with your current employer
Recruiters ask for it
To count rejections over time, which keeps you motivated and shows recruiters how persistent you have been throughout
resume-apply:3.explanation: Conversion rates per stage tell you what to improve: resume (few screens), coding (fail technicals), or system design/behavioral (fail onsites). It's a diagnostic tool.

resume-apply:3.prompt: You get an offer from Company A with a 3-day deadline while Company B is mid-process and is your top choice. What's the best move?
options: Accept A immediately and stop B
Reject A to focus on B
Accept A now, then quietly back out later if B comes through, without telling A until you've decided
Tell B about the deadline and ask if they can expedite, and ask A politely for a short extension
resume-apply:3.explanation: Companies often accelerate for candidates with competing offers, and modest extensions are common requests. Accepting then reneging burns bridges, and rejecting A gives up your leverage.

resume-apply:3.prompt: Which habits make an application phase effective? Select all that apply.
options: Applying in focused batches with referrals where possible
Continuing DSA and system design practice while interviewing
Writing a short retro after each interview round
Stopping all preparation once applications are submitted
resume-apply:3.explanation: Batching, ongoing practice and retros compound across interviews. Stopping preparation lets skills decay just as interviews start.

resume-apply:3.prompt: After an interview loop rejection, which actions are productive? Select all that apply.
options: Politely ask the recruiter for any feedback
Note which questions or rounds went poorly and practice them
Ask about the cool-off period to reapply later
Argue with the recruiter that the decision was wrong
resume-apply:3.explanation: Feedback, targeted practice and knowing reapply timelines turn rejections into progress. Arguing rarely changes decisions and can damage future chances.

resume-apply:3.prompt: It's generally better to start applying once you're reasonably prepared rather than waiting until you feel 100% ready.
options: True
False
resume-apply:3.explanation: True. Real interviews give feedback that practice can't, and hiring processes take weeks. Waiting for perfect readiness delays the loop; a sensible warm-up order manages the risk.

resume-apply:3.prompt: Using exactly the same generic resume and no referrals for every application is the most efficient approach, because volume matters more than targeting.
options: True
False
resume-apply:3.explanation: False. Untargeted, high-volume applying usually yields low callback rates. Referrals plus light tailoring typically convert far better per application.
